strengths: Proposes a novel visual GUI world model for App agents, addressing an important limitation of language-only world models by predicting future GUI observations as images.

Introduces Symbolic Text Representation (STR) to decouple graphic and text generation, using diffusion for placeholder layout and an LLM for text content, which is a sensible way to handle GUI text rendering fidelity.
Integrates the world model into an App-agent decision loop, where predicted next GUIs are used to select better actions, and reports consistent improvement across several agents.
Provides a reasonably broad set of experiments: GUI quality, trajectory synthesis, agent decision optimisation, and ablations on static text and action instruction conditioning.
Appendix includes detailed prompts and pipeline descriptions, which improves clarity and some reproducibility.
Qualitative examples illustrate the approach's ability to generate plausible GUI transitions and generalise to some novel action combinations.
weaknesses: The evaluation uses the same 19 Apps across training, validation, and test splits, so there is no measurement of generalisation to unseen Apps. This is a major gap for a real-world App world model, where deployment would require handling new applications.

Many central metrics rely on LLM-as-a-judge, including instructional accuracy, action readiness, trajectory matching, and agent step accuracy. There is no human validation, no inter-judge agreement analysis, and no direct OCR/text-fidelity metric, even though text generation is the core novelty.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair or under-specified: UI-diffuser is not inherently action-conditioned, IP2P is an image-editing model, and it is unclear whether baselines were fine-tuned on the same data with comparable compute and hyperparameters.

The STR pipeline is brittle and heavily handcrafted: it relies on OCR, colour/boundary detection for white-filled/black-bordered rectangles, and heuristics/LLM filtering for static text. It may fail on diverse real GUIs with gradients, transparency, dark mode, non-rectangular text, or unusual styling.
The agent-enhancement procedure requires generating multiple future GUIs per step, but inference cost, latency, and scaling behaviour are not analysed.

Claims such as 'first visual GUI world model' and large relative improvements need stronger support; gains over the best visual baselines in agent tasks are modest and measured only in a limited same-App setting.
No real emulator or execution-based evaluation is provided. The method is evaluated using predicted GUIs and simulated actions, so compounding errors and real-world action outcomes remain unverified.
Minor clarity and reproducibility issues exist: typos such as 'VisMo', 'APP-Agnet', 'Langugae', and the project link is missing, with no code/model release details.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and timely problem: enabling App agents with a visual world model rather than text-only future-state prediction.
Proposes a practical pipeline (STR) that decouples GUI generation into graphic layout prediction via diffusion and text content generation via an LLM.
Includes multiple evaluation angles: GUI quality, trajectory synthesis, and enhancement of existing App agents, plus ablation studies on design choices.
Reports improvements in step-wise action prediction and trajectory synthesis over several baselines, supported by qualitative visual examples.
Appendix provides substantial implementation detail, including prompts and dataset construction, improving transparency.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: decomposing GUI generation into graphics plus text placeholders and delegating text rendering to an LLM is intuitive and close to existing layout/text-rendering pipelines.
The 'first visual GUI world model' claim is overclaimed and not adequately positioned against prior UI generation, image-editing, and world-model work.

Main evaluation is limited: results are shown on a small sampled subset, and the improvement over the strongest baseline (HTML-vision) in GUI quality is only about 5.39% harmonic relative gain, while the 29.14% average is inflated by a weak UI-diffuser baseline.
The central metrics s_ia and s_ar rely on LLM judges without human validation or reliability analysis, and DINO similarity may not capture functional GUI correctness.
No task success or completion rate is reported; step-wise action accuracy does not directly support the paper's long-horizon planning claim.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair or incomplete: HTML-vision conversion could understate its performance, and strong action-conditioned text-rendering baselines such as TextDiffuser-2 are not quantitatively compared.

Technical details around deployment are underspecified: how action instructions are obtained from real agent outputs, how action options are generated, and how the selection model is trained or calibrated.
Robustness is questionable: text-symbol detection assumes exact black-border/white-fill placeholders, diffusion may not reliably produce them, and failure cases are acknowledged but not quantified.
Static text is retained as image pixels, so the method still requires diffusion to generate some text, partially contradicting the motivation that pixel-level text generation is the core problem.
Reproducibility is limited: no code or working project link is provided, and key data filtering, training, and evaluation details are relegated to the appendix.
Generalization evidence is mostly qualitative; the paper does not quantify performance on novel action/app combinations or discuss ethical/privacy concerns around GUI datasets.

strengths: Introduces a novel visual GUI world model and the Symbolic Text Representation (STR), effectively addressing the text-distortion problem in pixel-level GUI generation by decomposing graphics and text generation.
Provides a reasonably broad evaluation suite covering GUI quality, trajectory synthesis, agent decision-making, and ablations on static text handling and action representation.
Demonstrates consistent improvements across several metrics and agent backbones, including a reported 14.07% relative step-accuracy gain for T3A, supporting the practical utility of the approach.
weaknesses: Potential target leakage: for AITW, action instructions are generated using the next screenshot (Appendix G.6), so the model may receive privileged information about the target state. This weakens claims that action instructions are inherently superior and may inflate main results.

Evaluation relies heavily on LLM-as-a-judge metrics and DINO similarity, without human evaluation or validation of the judges. Functional correctness, text readability, and user-perceived plausibility are not directly measured.

Improvements over the strongest baselines are sometimes modest (e.g., ViMo vs. HTML-vision in GUI harmonic score and agent decision accuracy), and the headline 29.14% average gain is driven partly by a weak UI-diffuser baseline.

The dataset covers only 19 apps and sampled episodes; reproducibility is limited by missing implementation details such as exact LLM versions, training hyperparameters, compute, model sizes, and code availability.

The STR pipeline depends on OCR, rectangle detection, and LLM-based static-text filtering, which may be brittle for real-world GUIs with transparent, overlapping, stylized, multi-line, or non-rectangular text.

strengths: Introduces a new task setting: a visual GUI world model that predicts future App GUI images conditioned on current GUI and user action, going beyond language-only world models.

Proposes Symbolic Text Representation (STR), a simple but effective idea that decouples GUI graphic generation from text content generation, using placeholders to avoid pixel-level text rendering errors.
Comprehensive evaluation: automatic metrics, large user study, agent decision-making enhancement across multiple agents/world models, zero-shot generalization, and online navigation tasks.
Shows consistent improvements over strong baselines on GUI quality, step accuracy, and task success rates, with ablations validating STR components and action-instruction conditioning.
Practical deployment considerations are discussed, including lightweight model size, plug-and-play API, inference time, and safety/access safeguards.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: the method composes existing components (Stable Diffusion/IP2P, OCR, LLM prompting) with a simple overlay-based STR representation; the core contribution is more system-level than methodological.
The 'first visual GUI world model' claim is somewhat overstated, since fine-tuned image-editing models such as IP2P* are already adapted as visual world-model baselines.
Evaluation gaps remain: TextDiffuser-2 is shown qualitatively but omitted from the main quantitative comparisons, and other relevant scene-text or GUI-generation baselines are not fully explored.

Automatic metrics rely heavily on DINO similarity and LLM judges; although a user study supplements them, statistical significance, inter-annotator agreement, and possible bias in volunteer evaluation are not reported.

Reproducibility is limited: the dataset, training hyperparameters, model checkpoints, and exact data splits are not fully specified or openly released, and the pipeline depends on proprietary LLMs like GPT-4o.

Technical brittleness is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed: STR detection/diffusion failures, LLM text hallucination, and error accumulation over iterative rollouts can affect real-world reliability.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and challenging problem: visual world modeling for GUI/app agents, moving beyond text-only world models.
The proposed Symbolic Text Representation (STR) is a reasonable engineering idea: decoupling GUI graphics and text generation by masking text with placeholders and delegating text content to an LLM.
The method is integrated into existing App agents as a plug-and-play component, with experiments on GUI quality, agent decision-making, zero-shot generalization, and online navigation.
The empirical study includes automatic metrics, user studies, and ablations, which provides some evidence for the effectiveness of the approach in a few settings.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core pipeline combines existing components—diffusion-based image editing, OCR-based text masking, and LLM text prediction—rather than introducing a fundamentally new formulation or learning paradigm.

The evaluation of the world model is not sufficiently rigorous for the central claim. Automatic metrics rely heavily on LLM-as-judge and DINO similarity, but there is no direct evaluation of exact generated text accuracy, element-level correctness, or functional equivalence beyond downstream task accuracy.

The action-selection procedure introduces a major confounding factor: gains may come from the LLM-based candidate scoring and comparison rather than from ViMo’s predicted GUIs. The paper does not cleanly ablate the world model from the selection strategy.

Baseline comparisons are not fully convincing: UI-diffuser is not originally a next-GUI world model, IP2P* is fine-tuned but may not be a fair action-conditioned next-frame baseline, and language-based world models are adapted from web settings. Fairness of adaptation is insufficiently justified.

Reproducibility is limited. The abstract contains an incomplete project link, training/implementation details are sparse, and the model depends heavily on proprietary LLMs and diffusion models. Checkpoint access is restricted, reducing reproducibility.
The claimed real-world/online applicability is weakened by the reported inference time of roughly 2 minutes per request, which is not compatible with real-time interactive navigation.

The static-text ablation does not clearly support the stated conclusion: retaining static text alone actually degrades performance, and the improvement mainly appears when combined with action instructions, suggesting an interaction effect that is not fully analyzed.

The paper overstates its contributions and practical impact relative to the strength of the evidence, especially in claiming visually plausible and functionally effective GUIs without exact text or structure-level validation.

strengths: Targets an important and timely problem: enabling App agents to perform long-horizon planning via visual GUI world models, where prior work largely uses text-only or HTML-based world models.

Proposes a sensible and novel decomposition of GUI generation into graphic and text content, using Symbolic Text Representation (STR) to replace text with placeholders and delegate actual text generation to an LLM. This is a practical way to avoid diffusion-based text rendering artifacts.

Provides a broad empirical evaluation: GUI generation quality, user study, agent decision-making, zero-shot generalization, online AndroidWorld navigation, and ablations. The reported gains over baselines are consistent across multiple settings.
Shows meaningful downstream utility: ViMo improves M3A/T3A step accuracy and online task completion, suggesting the world model is not only visually plausible but functionally useful for agents.
Includes implementation details, prompts, dataset construction, and deployment considerations in the appendix, which improves transparency.
The work is clearly written and well organized, with useful qualitative visualizations and ablation studies on key design choices such as static text retention and action instruction conditioning.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate: the core idea of decomposing graphics and text is intuitive, and the diffusion+LLM pipeline is largely an engineering integration of existing components. The claim of being the 'first' visual GUI world model needs stronger positioning against prior GUI generation and web world-model work.

Text generation accuracy is not directly and independently evaluated. The final GUI metrics may conflate graphic quality, layout fidelity, and text correctness, and the LLM-based automatic metrics may be biased or hallucinated. A more rigorous text-content accuracy metric would strengthen the claims.

Reproducibility is limited: the project link is missing/incomplete, no code or model checkpoints are provided, and the method depends heavily on proprietary LLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini) with prompt-only descriptions. This makes exact reproduction difficult.

The action selection procedure is somewhat ad hoc: it uses two-stage LLM scoring and a comparison of the top two actions, motivated by an unsubstantiated observation that >70% of tasks have close top scores. This heuristic is not systematically validated.

Some main experiments use a relatively small sampled subset (57 episodes) rather than the full test split. Although full-split results are provided in the appendix, the main quantitative claims rely on a limited evaluation.

Baseline fairness is not fully established: fine-tuning details for IP2P* and UI-diffuser are limited, and HTML-vision rendering may introduce confounds. Comparisons with language-based world models also need tighter control.

Practical efficiency is a concern: total inference time is reported as about 2 minutes per request on a V100, which may be too slow for real-time online navigation, despite the online evaluation. The latency/accuracy trade-off deserves more discussion.

Failure cases of STR are acknowledged but not quantified. OCR errors, incorrect placeholder detection, and unrecognizable text symbols can propagate, yet the paper does not report the frequency or impact of these failures.
